narrative: The model estimated a 65% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain, but under the admission process it was high enough to lead to rejection. The strongest reason was your third-year class rank: you are in the second decile, while accepted students average around the sixth decile. This low rank pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure. The next most important factor was your LSAT score of 39, slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, and this pushed the prediction toward passing. Your first-year class rank was the third most influential factor: you were in the third decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, and this also pushed toward failure, though less strongly than your third-year rank. Because two of the three most influential factors, especially your third-year academic standing, pointed toward failure, the overall prediction remained above the rejection threshold. To strengthen a future application, focus on improving your academic record, particularly upper-year grades and class rank; consider retaking the LSAT if you can raise it further; speak with an admissions or academic advisor about how to address past grades; and apply to a balanced range of schools where your profile is more competitive.
